questions.title: The questions behind most *projects*
questions.lead: A first call usually starts with one of these. Bring yours.

pairs.q: Should we build this ourselves or buy a platform?
pairs.a: The answer usually sits in three numbers: what the process costs today, what a platform costs over three years, and how different your process really is. A discovery sprint puts figures on all three before any contract is signed.

pairs.q: Our pilot worked. Why is nobody using it?
pairs.a: Stalled pilots usually lack an owner and a rollout plan, not features. The first step is to name who has to change what, set one adoption metric, and support the first weeks of use.

pairs.q: Are our data and KPIs ready for AI?
pairs.a: Not until two people give the same answer to the same KPI. Definitions and ownership come first, then data quality, then the AI use case.

faq.title: What teams ask before they *hire us*

items.q: Do you only advise, or do you also build?
items.a: Both. Advice, design, build and operations support can be bought separately or as one engagement. [Describe the engineering model: in-house or vetted partners.]

items.q: How do you work with our own team and vendors?
items.a: We join your meetings and tools, keep one shared backlog and name one owner per release. Where you already have vendors, we assess fit and manage the hand-offs instead of replacing them by default.
Run and support covers rollout, training, monitoring and a monthly improvement review, scoped as a retainer. The first review sets the numbers we track together.

items.q: How long does a discovery sprint take?
items.a: Two to four weeks. It ends with a scoped plan, a build-or-buy analysis and a clickable prototype.

items.q: Can you work in Vietnamese and English?
items.a: Yes. Workshops, documents and handover are available in both languages. English is the source for written deliverables.
Each engagement model has a starting price on the pricing page. Scope sets the final figure and is agreed before work starts.
